chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The House Next Door
chapters.artPrompt: a rooftop of grey London leads at dawn with curling chimney smoke, a thin girl in a patched black dress standing between chimney stacks, gazing down at the warmly lit windows of a grand house next door, an Indian servant in a white turban visible at a lower window, soft golden morning light over cold blue rooftops, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The days after the feast were the hardest Sara had ever known. Miss Minchin watched her like a hawk, and found fault with everything she did. But Sara kept one bright secret place. Every fine morning she climbed out on the leads of the attic roof, and looked down at the warm, busy house next door.
From the rooftop leads, Sara watches the windows of the house next door.

That house was full of strange life now. There was Mr. Carrisford, the sad Indian gentleman, lying on his sofa by a bright fire. There was Ram Dass, his quick and gentle servant, who wore a white turban and moved over the roofs like a cat. And there was a little monkey, who did exactly as he pleased all day long, and was never once sorry.
New word: turban — a long cloth wound round the head. Ram Dass wore a snow-white one, and looked very grand indeed.

One afternoon the monkey gave the whole street a fright. He slipped out of a window, leaped across the roofs, and landed on Sara's attic windowsill. He chattered, pulled at her hair, and sat down as if the attic belonged to him. Then Ram Dass came over the roof after him, bowing and smiling, and Sara laughed for the first time in many days.

Ram Dass knew a little English, and Sara knew a few words of his own tongue. They talked of India — of temples, and tigers, and the smell of the first warm rain. 'Missee Sahib,' he said, 'you look like a princess out of a story.' 'That is what I try to be,' said Sara, smiling. 'Even up here, even in the cold.'

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · What Melchisedec Heard
chapters.artPrompt: a cold grey attic interior with a small girl in a patched dress sitting on the floorboards against the wall, talking with her hands folded, a little grey rat sitting up and listening beside a hole in the wainscot, faint snow light through a grimy window, quiet muted blues and browns, storybook illustration

blocks.text: That winter the attic cupboard was emptier than ever, and Sara's dinners were smaller than anyone guessed. One grey afternoon she sat on the floor with her back against the cold wall, and spoke aloud, as she often did, to keep her courage up. Speaking out loud made hunger seem much smaller than it was.
A hungry princess tells her dreams to a small grey listener.

In a hole in the wall lived a little grey rat, whom Sara had named Melchisedec. He crept out and sat up, whiskers twitching, and listened like a gentleman. 'Melchisedec,' said Sara, 'suppose there was a grand banquet, just once. Suppose there were hot buns, and roast things, and little iced cakes, and a fire like a little sun.'
New word: banquet — a splendid grand meal with many dishes, fit for a king. Sara only wished for one; she did not dream one was already coming.

But high on the roof, on the other side of the wall, someone else was listening. Ram Dass lay in the warm dark beside the skylight, and every hungry word went straight to his heart. That very night he told Mr. Carrisford, and Mr. Carrisford sat up in his chair. 'Do it,' he said. 'Let the child have her banquet, and let her never know who sent it.'

So a kind plan was made, quietly, on the other side of the wall. Sara fell asleep in the cold, dreaming of buns and fires and silver dishes. She never guessed that her dream was already coming true, one basketful at a time.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The Magic
chapters.artPrompt: a transformed attic interior at night glowing with warmth, a bright fire blazing in a small iron grate, a table set with steaming soup and pies and little cakes, thick blankets folded on an old armchair, a pair of soft red slippers on the floorboards, two amazed girls in the doorway, rose and amber light against blue shadows, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The next evening Sara came home late, wet, tired, and very hungry indeed. She opened the attic door — and stood quite still on the mat. A fire was blazing in the grate. On the table stood hot soup, and meat pies, and little cakes, and a kettle singing softly on the hob.
The cold attic transformed, as if by magic, while Sara was out.

On the old armchair lay thick warm blankets, and on the floor stood a pair of soft slippers, exactly Sara's size. She put out one cold hand and touched the kettle. It was hot. 'Oh, it is the Magic!' she whispered. 'I believe it is the Magic at last, and it has found me out.'
New word: grate — the iron frame at the bottom of a chimney, where the fire is laid. Sara's grate had been cold and empty for two long years.

She ran down for Becky, and the two sat by the fire and ate like two little queens. Every evening after that, new wonders appeared — a bright lamp, a hot supper, a warm coat for Becky. Sara always saved the best pieces and carried them out in a paper bag.

'For Ermengarde,' she said, 'and for anybody hungrier than we are. A princess always shares her magic.' And so she did, until the whole attic glowed like a palace, winter though it was, and the coldest room in London became the warmest.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · After the Feast
chapters.artPrompt: a tall Victorian schoolhouse back stairs in early morning grey light, a thin girl in a patched dress scrubbing stone steps with a bucket beside her, her breath showing in the cold, long shadows of banisters, a scolding silhouetted woman above, cold blue tones with one small warm coal glow, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The trouble from the birthday feast still followed Sara like a shadow. Miss Minchin blamed her for everything now, and gave her the dirtiest work in the house. Sara scrubbed steps, and carried coals, and ran errands through the rain, and was scolded whenever she came back.
The long grey days of work, warmed only by what the night brought back.

One morning she was sent to make the schoolroom fire before the sun was up. Her hands were red with cold, and her supper was a heel of bread. Becky was kept below stairs, and Lottie was not allowed near her. It was unjust, and Sara knew perfectly well that it was unjust.
New word: errand — a short job away from home, such as carrying a message or buying something small.

'They may take the fire and the supper,' she said to herself, standing very straight, 'but they cannot take what I am inside. I am still a princess, and princesses hold their heads up.' So she walked through the grey days with her chin high, and did every hard job as if it were a royal command.

And at night, when she climbed to the attic, the Magic was waiting. The fire leaped and the kettle sang, and the unjust day melted away like snow. Whatever Miss Minchin took away by day, something kind gave back twice as much by night.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · The Search in Moscow
chapters.artPrompt: a snowy Russian city square with onion-domed churches and a grand railway station, a tall English gentleman in a heavy fur-collared coat stepping from a sleigh with travel bags, lamplight on deep snow, a distant family with a little girl crossing the square, cold lavender evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Next door, Mr. Carrisford was growing sadder and thinner. For two whole years he had searched for his lost friend's little girl — through hospitals, and schools, and boarding-houses, in every city he could think of. There had been no news of her at all.

Now his friend Mr. Carmichael had sailed away to Moscow, chasing a new clue. A Russian family was travelling home with a little English girl, and perhaps — just perhaps — she was the child. The whole house waited, and even the monkey was quiet, and the fire seemed to burn softly, so as not to disturb the hoping.
Mr. Carmichael's long search takes him far across the snowy world.
New word: clue — a small sign that helps you solve a mystery, like a footprint left in snow.

At last the answer came, and it was a cold one. Mr. Carmichael wrote from Moscow: the little girl was the wrong one. It was not Sara Crewe. Mr. Carrisford turned his face to the wall. 'I cannot look for her any more,' he said. 'I am too tired, and my heart is too heavy.'
But that very night, a storm was rising over London. And up in the attic, a small wet monkey was squeezing himself through the skylight, out of the wind, and into the very story he belonged to.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 · The Monkey in the Storm
chapters.artPrompt: a dark attic under sloping eaves in a wild night storm, a small soaked monkey wrapped in a warm blanket held by a girl in a patched dress beside a glowing fire, rain lashing a slanted skylight above, shingles rattling, deep blue night with one island of amber firelight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: It was the wildest night of the whole winter. The wind howled down the chimneys, and the rain dashed against the roof like handfuls of gravel. Sara lay listening to it, half asleep, when she heard a small, miserable sound quite close to her bed.
A small wet monkey squeezes in from the storm through the skylight.

The monkey had run away from home, and he was soaked to the skin and shivering. Sara wrapped him in a warm blanket and held him by the fire till his fur stood up in a fluffy halo. 'You naughty, dear thing,' she said. 'You must go home in the morning, whatever the weather does.'
New word: skylight — a window set flat in a roof, to let the sky in. This one let in the sky, the rain, and one very wet monkey.

Morning came grey and drizzling. Sara carried the monkey down from the roof and across to the next-door house, holding her old shawl over them both. Ram Dass opened the door, and his face lit up like a lamp. The monkey leaped into his arms, chattering his whole adventure at once.

And through the doorway, in a big chair by the fire, a thin gentleman sat watching Sara with strange, fast-beating eyes. Something about her voice had already begun to stir a memory he could not quite reach.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 · The Child He Used to Know
chapters.artPrompt: a richly furnished Victorian drawing room with a deep glowing fire, a thin gentleman in a dressing gown leaning forward from his chair with hands clasped and eyes full of tears, a ragged little girl in a patched black dress standing straight with her chin high, warm firelight on both faces, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Mr. Carrisford could not take his eyes off her. She was ragged and cold, but she stood like a little queen, and something about her tugged at his heart. 'Will you sit by the fire a moment, child?' he said gently. 'Tell me about the monkey, and about the attic where you live.'
By the fire, a tired gentleman looks and looks at a ragged little girl.

So Sara sat in the warm glow and talked — of Becky, and Emily, and the Bastille, and the magic suppers. Her voice was low and kind, and it was like a voice he had heard long ago, in another country, in a happier life. He leaned closer and closer, hardly breathing.

'What is your name?' he asked at last. 'Sara Crewe,' she said. Then there was a cry. Mr. Carrisford was on his feet, holding both her hands, and the tears were running down his face. 'It is the child!' he called. 'The child I used to know — the child I have been seeking all the world over!'
New word: seeking — looking for with all your heart, and never giving up. Mr. Carrisford had been seeking Sara for two years.

Sara stood wondering, too astonished to speak. A princess in a story would have known exactly what to say. But before she could find any words at all, Mr. Carmichael came hurrying in from the hall, and the whole house began to tremble with joy.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 · I Tried Not to Be
chapters.artPrompt: a warm lamplit study with a glowing fire and leather chairs, a gentleman in a dressing gown telling a story with open hands while a ragged little girl sits on a footstool listening, tears and smiles together, a lawyer gentleman smiling in the doorway, amber and rose light on bookshelves, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Then they told her everything, gently and slowly, the way you tell wonderful news. The diamond mines were real, and they were rich beyond counting. Her father had put all his money into them, and had died believing they had failed — but they had not. Every penny of it was Sara's now.
The story of the diamond mines, told at last, with a happy ending.

'Your father was my dearest friend,' said Mr. Carrisford. 'I ran away from him when he was ill, and I have been hunting for his little girl ever since, to pay my debt. Now I have found you, Sara, and I shall never, never let you go.' And Mr. Carmichael nodded, and blew his nose very loudly.

Sara sat very still, and two great tears fell. 'The day they told me he was gone,' she said, 'I tried not to be anything. I tried not to care. But I did care, all the time.' And Mr. Carrisford took her in his arms like a father, and the fire crackled for joy.
New word: heiress — a person who will have a great deal of money, left by someone who loved them.

So the lost little girl was found, and the beggar-child of the attic was an heiress. But when they asked her how she had lived through it all, she only said, 'I pretended I was a princess. And then, at last, it came true.'

chapters.title: Chapter 17 · Becky Comes Too
chapters.artPrompt: an attic landing at the top of a narrow staircase in bright morning light, a ragged girl in a crooked cap sitting flat on the floor crying happy tears while a dark-haired girl in a patched dress laughs beside her, a small monkey patting the ragged girl's shoulder, sunlight streaming down the stairwell, storybook illustration

blocks.text: There was one thing Sara would not leave behind, and it was not the attic, and it was not the roof. 'Becky comes with me,' she said. 'She has been my friend in the cold. Wherever I go, Becky goes.' So Becky was sent for, and came up from the kitchen with her cap crooked and her eyes like saucers.
Sara and Becky leave the attic together, friends for always.

'Me, miss!' Becky gasped. 'Me — to live along of YOU?' 'You are not to say miss any more,' laughed Sara. 'You are to say Sara.' And Becky sat down flat on the attic floor and cried for happiness, while the monkey patted her shoulder very kindly indeed.
New word: companion — a friend who goes with you and shares your days. Becky was to be Sara's own companion, and a lady's maid besides.

They went down the attic stairs together for the very last time. Lottie flung herself at Sara, and Ermengarde hugged her till the buttons creaked, and even the smallest girls stopped their lessons to wave out of the window at the two friends.

Miss Minchin stood at the door with a face like stone, saying what she was told to say. Sara looked at her kindly. 'I shall not be cross with you,' she said. 'Perhaps someday you will be sorry. Goodbye.' And the two friends walked out into the sunshine together.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 · The Great Clearing
chapters.artPrompt: a bright new bedroom with white curtains and a crackling fire, a dark-haired girl in a fine blue dress unpacking books and a French doll, a cheerful ragged-turned-neat girl making up a bed, a small monkey on the bedpost, boxes and roses everywhere, sunny morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Next morning, carts and servants came to the school, and the great clearing began. Sara's own room was made bright and new, with books, and roses, and a fire that never went out. Next door, a warm little room was got ready for Becky, with a bed all her own.
The clearing-out, and the bright new life next door.

Miss Minchin ordered the empty attic swept and shut up, and made the best of a bad job. But the schoolroom whispered all day long. The princess had been in the attic all the time — and nobody had known it but the few who were kind to her.

Sara's new life was full to the brim. She had lessons in the morning, and tea with Mr. Carrisford in the afternoon, and Ram Dass to tell her stories of India. The monkey sat on her shoulder at breakfast. The children of the Large Family came running to play, and called her their fairy godmother.
New word: clearing-out — putting everything in order, and carrying away what is finished with. Some clearings-out end one story and begin a better one.

Ermengarde and Lottie still came across the square, hand in hand, and the four friends laughed at nothing and everything. 'It is like the stories I used to make up,' said Sara. 'Only this one is true — and I am in it.'

chapters.title: Chapter 19 · A Princess Still
chapters.artPrompt: a cozy London bun-shop interior with golden buns in rows behind the counter, a plump kind baker-woman in an apron handing a paper bag to a small ragged girl with big grateful eyes, a dark-haired girl in a fine coat watching from the doorway, warm lamplight and rising steam, storybook illustration

blocks.text: And what of Miss Minchin? She kept her school, and her manners, and her black silk dress. But she never dared be unkind again, for now the grandest families in London knew the story of the attic. When Sara passed her in the street, Miss Minchin bowed — and did not enjoy it one little bit.

Sara did not spend her fortune on fine things first. Her very first errand was to the bun-shop, where the kind baker-woman stood in the door. 'Have you the little girl still?' asked Sara. 'Anne? Yes, my dear, and a good worker too.' 'Then let her always have buns,' said Sara. 'And let any hungry child have them, forever, on my word.'
The bun-shop, where hungry children were fed forever after, and never knew why.
New word: fortune — a very great deal of money. Sara's fortune came from diamond mines, but her real riches had never cost a penny.

And so it was. On wet nights, children with no suppers crept into the warm bun-shop, and never knew whose kindness fed them. But Anne knew, and the baker-woman knew, and they blessed Sara's name quietly every single day.

As for Sara — she had her father's fortune, her father's friend, and her friends of the cold days too. She wore nice dresses now, but she was the same Sara. Princess or beggar, hungry or full, she was — and always would be — a princess still.
